The front and back focal lengths of a single spherical surface are always exactly equal to each other
The paraxial approximation is also known as Gaussian optics
10.2.explanation: The exact Snell's-law relation is transcendental; the paraxial (small-angle) approximation, also called Gaussian optics, yields the h-independent relation n1/so+n2/si=(n2-n1)/R; the notes explicitly show fo≠fi for a single interface, so front and back focal lengths are generally NOT equal.

10.4.stem: Which of the following are correct about image formation for off-axis object points, as derived in this section? (Select all that apply)
options: The thin-lens equation 1/so + 1/si = 1/f also holds for object points off the optical axis (yo ≠ 0)
Newton's formula relates the object and image distances from the focal points as xo·xi = f²
The transverse magnification is MT = yi/yo = −si/so
The longitudinal magnification ML relates to the transverse magnification via ML = −MT²
The three chief rays used to trace image formation through an ideal lens are only valid for concave (diverging) lenses
10.4.explanation: The lens equation extends to off-axis points, Newton's formula xo·xi=f² and the magnification relations MT=-si/so and ML=-MT² are all correctly derived; the three chief-ray construction is a general technique for ideal lenses, not restricted to concave ones.

10.5.stem: Which of the following are correct about systems of two thin lenses, as derived in this section? (Select all that apply)
options: For two thin lenses in contact (separation d≈0), the combined focal length satisfies 1/f = 1/f1 + 1/f2
Equivalently, using lens powers, the combined power is D = D1 + D2
The overall magnification of a two-lens system is the product of each lens's individual magnification, MT = MT1·MT2
In lens systems generally (e.g. thick lenses), front and back focal lengths must be redefined relative to the whole system
Combining lenses made of different materials can never help reduce chromatic aberration
10.5.explanation: The combined-focal-length and lens-power addition rules, the multiplicative magnification MT1·MT2, and the need to redefine front/back focal lengths for lens systems are all correctly derived; the notes explicitly describe using different-dispersion materials (doublets/triplets) specifically to REDUCE chromatic aberration.

10.6.stem: Which of the following are correct about apertures, stops, and pupils in an optical system, as introduced in this section? (Select all that apply)
options: The aperture stop (AS) restricts the total amount of light propagating through the system
The field stop (FS) restricts the size of the image, rather than the amount of light
The entrance pupil is the image of the aperture stop as seen from object space
The exit pupil is the image of the aperture stop as seen from image space
Aperture stops and field stops always refer to the exact same physical component in a system
10.6.explanation: The aperture stop (light quantity) and field stop (image size) are distinct components; the entrance and exit pupils are the images of the aperture stop as seen from object space and image space respectively — the two stops are conceptually and often physically distinct components, not always the same one.

10.7.stem: Which of the following are correct about mirrors, as introduced in this section? (Select all that apply)
options: A flat mirror forms a virtual image that is the mirror image of the object, reversing its handedness
A spherical mirror obeys the same lens-equation form 1/so+1/si=1/f, with f ≡ −R/2
The transverse magnification for a mirror is defined the same way as for lenses, MT = yi/yo
Unlike lenses, mirrors are largely free of chromatic aberration since their behavior doesn't depend much on wavelength
It is generally easier to manufacture very large lenses than very large mirrors
10.7.explanation: The flat-mirror handedness reversal, the spherical-mirror lens-equation form with f=-R/2, the mirror magnification MT=yi/yo, and mirrors' near-wavelength-independence (hence low chromatic aberration) are all correctly described; the notes state it's actually easier to manufacture large MIRRORS than large lenses, not the reverse.

10.8.stem: Which of the following are correct about prisms, as introduced in this section? (Select all that apply)
options: A prism's behavior can be based on refraction at the interfaces of a dispersive medium
A prism's behavior can alternatively be based on total internal reflection at a prism-air interface
Prisms can be used, like diffraction gratings, to separate different frequency components of light (e.g. in spectrometers)
Prisms can be used to guide/reflect broadband light with low losses, or to flip images (e.g. in binoculars)
Prisms exploit exactly the same physical mechanism as diffraction gratings to disperse light
10.8.explanation: Refraction-based dispersion and TIR-based reflection are the two prism mechanisms described, used respectively for spectral separation and for lossless broadband guiding/image-flipping; prisms disperse light via material dispersion (wavelength-dependent refractive index), a different physical mechanism from a grating's periodic interference.

10.9.stem: Which of the following are correct about the optics of the human eye, as introduced in this section? (Select all that apply)
options: Light is most strongly refracted at the air-cornea interface, where the refractive-index contrast is largest
The eye's ability to focus on both near and far objects is called accommodation
The iris adjusts the amount of light entering the eye, acting as a variable aperture stop
Rod cells sense color but not intensity, while cone cells sense intensity but not color
The fovea centralis is the retinal location where the sharpest vision occurs
10.9.explanation: Strongest refraction at the cornea, accommodation, the iris as a variable aperture stop, and the fovea centralis as the sharpest-vision location are all correctly described; the notes state the OPPOSITE role split — rod cells sense intensity (enabling night vision) but not color, while cone cells sense both intensity and color.

10.10.stem: Which of the following are correct about the magnifying glass (simple magnifier), as derived in this section? (Select all that apply)
options: A magnifying glass increases the apparent angular size of an object by allowing it to be brought closer to the eye than the unaided near point permits
Ideally, a magnifying glass forms a virtual image infinitely far from the eye
The angular magnification of a simple magnifier is MP = do/f = do·D, where D is the lens power
Using an arbitrarily short focal length gives arbitrarily large useful magnification, with no practical downside
Any positive (converging) lens can, in principle, act as a magnifying glass
10.10.explanation: The magnifier's angular-magnification mechanism MP=do/f=do·D, the virtual-image-at-infinity design goal, and any converging lens's ability to act as one are all correctly described; the notes explicitly note that lens aberrations limit how much useful magnification a simple magnifier can practically achieve.

10.11.stem: Which of the following are correct about instruments designed to be used directly by the human eye, as introduced in this section on the eyepiece? (Select all that apply)
options: In the simplest case, such an instrument consists of an objective lens and an eyepiece (ocular)
The objective lens forms an intermediate image between the two lenses
The eyepiece is placed one focal length away from the intermediate image
The purpose of the eyepiece is to further magnify the intermediate image for viewing by the eye
In this two-lens layout, the objective and eyepiece must always have identical focal lengths
10.11.explanation: The two-lens (objective + eyepiece) layout, the objective's intermediate image, the eyepiece's placement one focal length away, and its magnifying role are all correctly described; nothing requires the two lenses to share the same focal length — in fact their differing focal lengths set the overall magnification.
